content: Sudden Unexpected Death Syndrome (SUDS), known as bangungot in the Philippines, lai tai in Thailand, and hukuri in Japan, refers to the sudden and unexpected death of adolescents and adults during sleep. This phenomenon is rarely observed in Western countries but is more commonly reported among young men in East and Southeast Asia. The term bangungot originates from the Tagalog word for bad dream, as survivors often describe experiencing vivid dreams of falling into a bottomless pit. During these episodes, individuals are aware they are dreaming but feel paralyzed, unable to move or wake up. In many cultures, SUDS has been surrounded by superstitions. In Thailand, it is believed to be associated with consuming rice cakes, while in the Philippines, it is thought to result from eating large amounts of carbohydrates before sleeping. However, scientific understanding of this syndrome has only recently begun to emerge. Victims of SUDS typically do not have any detectable organic or structural heart diseases. However, during SUDS episodes, cardiac monitoring has revealed irregular heart rhythms, including ventricular fibrillation. Survival depends on whether the heart's rhythm spontaneously returns to normal. In the Philippines, traditional advice suggests wiggling the big toe during an episode to snap out of the condition. Modern research, led by Spanish electrophysiologist Dr. Josep Brugada Terradellas, has identified mutations in the cardiac sodium channel gene as a cause of SUDS. This genetic mutation, which affects the electrical activity of the heart, is inherited, explaining why the condition often runs in families. In the Philippines, many cases of bangungot have been linked to Acute Hemorrhagic Pancreatitis, while in Thailand and Laos, the condition is more commonly associated with Brugada syndrome, a genetic disorder affecting the heart's electrical system. In Filipino folklore, bangungot is also personified as a mythological creature called the batibat, a hag-like entity that is said to sit on the victim's chest or face, immobilizing and suffocating them during sleep.
